pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Define SLI, SLO, and error budget in your own words — and tell me why 100% is the wrong availability target for almost any service.
expected_points: SLI: a metric standing for user experience, canonically good events / valid events per user journey
SLO: a target for an SLI over a window, chosen from user need and measured baseline; the error budget is 1 minus the SLO — failure you are allowed
100% is imperceptible past the user's own network and each nine costs roughly 10x; a system that must never break can never change

questions.prompt: A service holds a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days at 1,000 requests/s. Work out the error budget in minutes and in requests — and what does the team do differently when the budget runs out?
expected_points: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is about 43 minutes of full outage
about 2.6 billion requests per 30 days, so roughly 2.6 million allowed failures; partial outages spend it fractionally
budget as policy: while it lasts you spend it on risk (deploys, experiments); exhausted budget freezes releases in favor of reliability work

questions.prompt: Why should pages fire on symptoms (user impact) rather than causes like CPU or cache hit ratio — and what actually happens to a team whose pager is wired to causes?
expected_points: a page must mean users are affected and a human must act now; causes are many, weakly correlated with impact, often self-healing
noisy pages train the on-call to ignore the pager (alert fatigue), so the real incident gets muted or detected by customers
causes still belong on dashboards consulted after a symptom pages, or in tickets when predictive (e.g. disk filling)

questions.prompt: Walk me through a well-run incident from first page to closed postmortem. Where does diagnosis fit, and what makes the postmortem blameless without being consequence-free?
expected_points: detect (ideally a burn-rate page), mitigate first — roll back on change-correlated impact before understanding why — communicate on a cadence, diagnose after users are healthy
blameless: assume competent people acting on the information they had and ask why the system allowed it; multiple contributing factors, not one root cause
accountability lives in action items with an owner and a deadline that close detection, mitigation, prevention, or communication gaps

questions.prompt: Your service synchronously calls a third-party notification API that just started hanging until its 10-second timeout. Which degradation tools do you reach for, and why is retrying harder the wrong first move?
expected_points: the dependency is non-critical: take it off the critical path (async via a queue) and fail open — drop or delay notifications rather than fail the user's action
circuit breaker: fail fast locally after a failure threshold, probe recovery via half-open, instead of burning the request's latency budget per call
retries amplify load on a struggling dependency (retry storms); if used at all they must be bounded, backed off, jittered, and budgeted

questions.prompt: Why do SLO-based pages use burn rates over multiple windows instead of a simple 'error rate above X for 5 minutes' threshold?
expected_points: burn rate normalizes error rate by the budget, so the alert speaks in budget consumed — the thing the SLO actually promises
a fast window (e.g. 14.4x over 1 h) catches outages in minutes while a slow window (e.g. 6x over 6 h) catches slow bleeds a short threshold misses
a short confirmation window makes the alert stop firing promptly once the issue is fixed

questions.prompt: Concretely, how does a blame-seeking postmortem culture make the next incident worse?
expected_points: people hide or shade exactly the information the analysis needs, so contributing factors go unfound and unfixed
the next engineer in the same situation has the same information and the same system, so the failure repeats regardless of who was blamed
fear slows incident response itself — hesitation to roll back, to escalate, or to declare an incident at all
